scenes.narration: Once you see Locke & Key as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. Locke & Key is an American comic book series written by Joe Hill, illustrated by Gabriel Rodríguez, and published by IDW Publishing. In 1775 during the American Revolution, a group of Rebels, hiding in a sea cave in Massachusetts Bay beneath what will one day be Keyhouse in the town of Lovecraft, discover a portal to another dimension, the plains of Leng.

The story Locke & Key tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. It is filled with demons who can mesmerize anyone who sees them and possess them through touch; two men are possessed over two days, and they kill several rebels. However, when the demons attempt to enter the real world without possessing someone, they are transformed into "whispering" iron, which young smith Benjamin Locke forges into a variety of magical keys.

Meaning is not found in Locke & Key — it is manufactured for it. The first key he makes is the Omega Key (which has an Omega character on the head) that seals the entrance to the dimension. The magic of the Keyhouse gradually evolves over the years, including a spell that causes occupants to forget about the keys and the magic of the house when they pass their 18th birthday.

The cold light on Locke & Key leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. Rendell Locke's younger brother Duncan follows the group into the cave, but he is mesmerized by demons in the open door, and attempts to walk through it. He is stopped by Lucas "Dodge" Caravaggio, who accidentally puts his hand through the doorway and is possessed by a demonic being.

Locke & Key did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. He plots to kill his friends and enslave the others; Dodge kills several and causes another to lose her memory. He also extracts a part of his spirit to be hidden in a jar in the home of Ellen "Ellie" Whedon, one of the surviving friends, as a contingency plan.

The honest version of Locke & Key starts by giving up the comforting part. Dodge is finally killed by Rendell before he can force more people to be possessed. Rendell discovers a small piece of "whispering" iron from the sea cave and disguises it as a fishing lure.

Strip Locke & Key of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. Around 2010, the fragment of Dodge's spirit partially possesses Ellie, who then conjures the rest of Dodge's spirit in the physical world at the magical well at Keyhouse, but Dodge is trapped within the well house. In 2011, Dodge's spirit reaches out to a young, abused prodigy, Sam Lesser, and convinces him to force Rendell to give him the Anywhere Key (which will allow Dodge to escape the wellhouse) and the Omega Key.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — Locke & Key shows exactly where that breaks. When Rendell refuses, Sam murders him, but Sam is then incapacitated by Tyler, Rendell's oldest son, and captured by the police. The Locke family, children Tyler, Kinsey, Bode, and mother Nina, move across the country to Keyhouse, reuniting with Duncan, and begin discovering the house's secrets.

What looks like free choice in Locke & Key is older than choice itself. Sam escapes prison with Dodge's help and follows the Lockes to Massachusetts. Sam attacks the family again at Keyhouse, but Dodge also tricks Bode into bringing him the Anywhere Key in case Sam fails again.

Nobody designed the part of Locke & Key you experience — it was inherited. Dodge escapes from the wellhouse with Bode's help, kills Sam, and returns to Lovecraft in the same body as he had thirty years before. Dodge intimidates his way into living in Ellie's home, who is now a teacher at the same high school she originally attended with Dodge, and where Tyler and Kinsey are enrolled; Dodge also re-enters the school under the guise of a new student and Ellie's cousin.

Every serious account of Locke & Key eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. Over the next year, Dodge secretly tries to recover the various keys – particularly the Omega Key – from the children, collecting many, though hindered by Tyler and Kinsey. Dodge is eventually discovered but manages to switch bodies and possesses Bode before they can kill him.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of Locke & Key — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. Now free to explore the house as Bode, Dodge finally finds the Omega Key and plans his takeover during the after-prom party in the sea cave. Dodge is ultimately undone by Tyler, having re-discovered the "whispering" iron from his father; he forges an "Alpha Key" with Duncan's help, which can exorcise a demon from the possessed soul, though it is fatal to the physical host.

The selfish-gene reading of Locke & Key makes it less romantic and far more precise. Dodge spirit in Bode's body is forced back into the well, killing the spirit again, though Bode's empty body is cremated before Bode's soul has a chance to return into it. In the epilogue, Tyler conjures Dodge's spirit again and uses the Alpha Key to finally exorcise Dodge from Lucas' soul, allowing Lucas' unpossessed soul to finally rest in death.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. Tyler uses the well's magic to speak with his father one last time. Finally, Tyler restores Bode's spirit to his physical form using the Animal Key.

The feeling that Locke & Key means something is a chemical event with an evolutionary address. The narrative of Locke & Key has a three-act structure, with each act covering two story arcs. Act One's first story arc, Welcome to Lovecraft, was a six-issue limited series published by IDW Publishing.

Nothing in Locke & Key was built for you — it was built for reproduction. The first issue of Welcome to Lovecraft was released on February 20, 2008, and sold out in a single day, requiring a second printing to be done immediately. The second arc of Act One, Head Games, commenced with the release of the first issue on January 22, 2009.

The psychology underneath Locke & Key is simpler and older than the story on top. The actual Head Games story was printed in four issues, with a standalone prologue ("Intermission" or "The Joe Ridgeway Story") and a standalone conclusion ("Army of One"). The first storyline of Locke & Key Act Two, Crown of Shadows, began in late 2009.

Behind Locke & Key sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. The first storyline of Act Three was announced as Time & Tide, but was retitled Clockworks. Originally, the plan was to release the first five-story arcs in a monthly format with the sixth arc published as an original graphic novel.

The nihilist does not deny Locke & Key — he only refuses to flatter it. The plan changed, and the concluding story arc appeared in monthly installments. In the universe of Locke & Key, there are many keys created from whispering iron that have different magical properties.

What culture calls destiny in Locke & Key is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. Some of them are extensively featured in the series, while others are featured very briefly. It instantly turns a demon into whispering iron, so if the demon is still inside the host, the key's effect is fatal.

The genes do not care about Locke & Key; they care about copies. Animal Key: Used on the right door in Keyhouse, it allows the user to travel through the door and transform into an animal. Animals may also transform into humans if they enter through the opposite side of the door.

Take away the meaning and Locke & Key still functions — that is the disturbing part. Anywhere Key: Opens a door to anywhere the bearer can visualize in their mind. Creation Key: Resembling a pencil, this key causes anything drawn with it to become real, living, or otherwise.

The unconscious does not argue with Locke & Key; it simply acts first. These things can also be erased by touching the other end of the key to them. Demon Key: When held against the spine of a person, a lock will appear.

Locke & Key feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. Echo Key: Allows entry to the Keyhouse wellhouse and, with the Echo Key in hand, allows a person to return a spirit from the dead to the world of the living. Leaving through the wellhouse door, however, banishes the spirit back to wherever it came from.

The bleak reading of Locke & Key is also the most testable one. This also applies to spirits that have possessed living bodies using the Ghost Key. Ghost Key: When used in the right door in Keyhouse, it separates the soul from the body of whoever travels through the door.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about Locke & Key. The body falls dead while their ghost is free to roam the Keyhouse grounds. Ghost souls can inhabit any other bodies nearby and clash with other ghosts.

The self that experiences Locke & Key is a committee, not a king. If the door is closed while the user is a ghost, they will become permanently separated from their own body. If the user is possessed by a demon, the demon will become visible when the user is a ghost, appearing to be physically attached to their spine.

Reproduction explains more of Locke & Key than any philosophy dares to admit. Giant Key: This physically large wooden key, once inserted into a keyhole-shaped window in Keyhouse, transforms the bearer into a massive giant. Head Key: Inserted into the base of someone's head, it allows one to peer inside the mind of a person, where memories and mental concepts (including "sanity" itself) are represented as tiny beings.

Once you see Locke & Key as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. Books inserted into a head with the Head Key transfer their contents to the bearer of the key, though in such a situation, the knowledge of the text is accurate but superficial. Hercules Key: Embedded in a necklace, it grants the bearer considerable strength and bulk.

The story Locke & Key tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. Identity Key: Upon inserting into the base of one's chin, the bearer can change any aspect of their appearance, including clothes, body, or even gender. However, the new appearance cannot match that of any existing person, and the user has to create a new face in their mind.

Meaning is not found in Locke & Key — it is manufactured for it. IDW Key: Opens an outhouse in the woods bearing the eye of the IDW Comics logo. Matchstick Key: Creates fires when inserted into a door or touched to an object, including a body.

The cold light on Locke & Key leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. Mending Key: Opens a magical cabinet in the Keyhouse into which a broken object can be placed (the cabinet can resize itself to the size of the object). While it can heal severely wounded people to some extent, it apparently cannot resurrect the dead.

Locke & Key did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. Mirror Key: When inserted into a mirror, it allows the user to open a doorway to a parallel-pocket universe, called the Prison of the Self. This key affects a mirror's reflection if it is held toward a mirror, as it makes the reflection eerily pleasant and beckons the person to enter.

The honest version of Locke & Key starts by giving up the comforting part. The user is then enticed to come into the mirror by their reflection, and upon entering, they find themselves in a dark, empty abyss. Moon Key: Allows the user to reach and open the Moon like a door, which allows the user to pass on to the afterlife peacefully.
